newsitem.title: USA: U.S. oil companies commit to Azerbaijan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. oil companies commit to Azerbaijan.

text.p: Four of the nation's biggest oil companies Friday signed deals said to be worth $8 billion to explore for and develop oil and gas properties in the Azerbaijani sector of the Caspian Sea.

Exxon Corp., Mobil Corp. and Chevron Corp. signed the production-sharing agreements with the State Oil Co. of the Azerbaijan Republic (SOCAR) during Azeri President Heydar Aliyev's visit to Washington, while Amoco Corp. signed a development agreement.
In production sharing, an oil company strikes a deal to split output, usually with a country's government or state-owned oil company.

Few details of the deal were given, apart from an $8 billion investment figure cited by Aliyev and potential reserves were not mentioned by the companies, which stressed the agreements were part of a long-range exploration program.

"While the structures on these blocks are believed to be very attractive prospects, drilling will be required to confirm the presence of any hydrocarbons," said Terry Koonce, president of Exxon Exploration and Production Azerbaijan Ltd.
The Department of Energy estimates total reserves in the Caspian Sea range from 90 billion to 200 billion barrels of oil.
Amoco's head of its Caspian Sea operations, Luke Keller, said that its Inam field, which is 125 miles offshore, could cost $2.5 billion to develop if it reached its full potential.
Russia's largest oil company, LUKoil, had wanted that field.

"Amoco has done a lot in Azerbaijan, such as spending on social projects, they deserve that field and have shown a great commitment to the region," said Julia Nanay of consulting firm Petroleum Finance Consultants.
Exxon won one property, the Nakhchivan block, about 60 miles south of Baku and said it was in talks over another deep-water block.

Mobil won a 50 percent stake in a block called Oguz, which is about 60 miles east of Baku, the Azeri capital, while Chevron got 50 percent of the Absheron Offshore Block which is in 250 about meters (825 feet) of water.
Both of these are close to the giant Guneshli-Azeri-Chirag fields.
Chevron expects to start drilling in late 1999, said Richard Matzke, head of Chevron Overseas Petroleum.
However, the U.S. oil giants do face some problems, even the new pipelines being planned are unlikely to have enough capacity to transport the oil out and there is a severe shortage of drilling rigs.
"These companies will probably have to get in more partners, especially if they have to bear the costs of SOCAR's side of the deal, and it is an extremely risky area," said PFC's Nanay.

The Caspian region, which is bordered five states, Azerbaijan, Russia, Iran, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan, is the subject of a dispute as to whether it is a sea or a lake, which affects its development.
Russia and Iran say that it is a lake and so should be developed jointly by all sides, but Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan say that it is a sea and should be split into separate territories.
The dispute surfaced again this week when Russian oil company Rosneft pulled out of a deal to develop with SOCAR a field called Kyapaz by the Azeris and Serdar by Turkmenistan.
Amoco's Keller said "that a sectoral division to promote rapid development" was in the best interests of those countries.
